title: LIFE IS COMING BACK: 11 Weeks in Gdansk
paragraphs: "LIFE IS COMING BACK" is a line from "Lovely" (1994) by 小沢健二, which I performed quite recently at the Nagoya University festival with the medical school light music club I belong to, and this is exactly the feeling I had during the 11 weeks I studied abroad. Whether this "LIFE" means life, vitality or something else entirely, I do not know, but whatever meaning I assign, I had this feeling. By repeating stimulating time in a foreign land spread out outside and quiet time spent alone in the dormitory and the library, I felt I had recovered something like the colors of life that I had been somehow about to forget.

Gdansk, a Polish city on the Baltic Sea. It has flourished since ancient times as an important trading port, and because of that geographical advantage it became the first target of Nazi Germany in 1939 and is the very place where the Second World War broke out; for me, who was originally strongly interested in the history of the first half of the twentieth century, it was a place I had wanted to visit at least once. Today Poland's economic growth is remarkable, and while retaining traces of the former Soviet Union here and there, it has a very interesting history and culture and a way of developing. As a result, everything I saw and touched was moving, and even now I truly think it was good that the first European city I visited was this Gdansk.

I landed in Gdansk about 20 hours after leaving Haneda Airport via Helsinki. After leaving the airport, I boarded a bus for the time being without knowing much about the rules of Poland's public transportation, was helped by a group of Black people on board, somehow reached the nearest bus stop, walked through a small forest, and arrived at a student dormitory with pale yellow walls reminiscent of the former Soviet era. There was no Wi-Fi, the gas stove could not be lit without a lighter, and when I arrived there was no refrigerator, so I was taken aback in various ways, but I got used to it quite quickly. Two or three days after I came to the dormitory, Professor Michael Wozniak of biochemistry, a pioneer of the exchange between the Medical University of Gdansk and Nagoya University, gave me food, tableware, kitchen supplies, clothespins and all sorts of things, and life suddenly became much more convenient. It is astonishing, and I cannot thank him enough, to think that he gives such generous support to Nagoya University students every year. As for eating habits, in Poland there is no concept of a proper lunch break, and the three basic meals are breakfast, dinner and supper. One eats bread brought along or at the cafeteria in free time, but I especially ate nothing during the clerkship and mostly bought something at the supermarket on the way home and cooked for myself in the dormitory. At the supermarket, vegetables and meat are not so different from Japan, but eggs cost nearly twice as much and were hard to afford, while fruit was quite cheap and very useful as a source of vitamins.

I had frequent opportunities to meet Professor Wozniak, who appeared above, in preparation for a certain important event. That was the two-day "Nagoya Days," held in early April at the university library and auditorium. It was an opportunity to communicate about Japan to local people from a medical perspective, and this year there were topics such as "the Japanese nurse 松澤フミ who saved Polish orphans left behind in Siberia after the First World War" and "the health effects of the polyphenols contained in green tea." To prepare for this event, we made presentations in cooperation with local students belonging to the Young Leaders Program (YLP), who were a group of students with very wide-ranging backgrounds, from undergraduates in biological fields at the University of Gdansk to nearby high school students including Professor Wozniak's grandchild, and since their upbringings and current fields of specialty differ from ours, we had very interesting conversations. As my return to Japan approached, one of the YLP students I had become friends with, who is studying Japanese, invited me to his home in the neighboring town of Sopot. We had a pleasant time talking about the future while eating Polish home cooking made by his mother and grandmother, and playing the guitar that was in his room together.

Now, to the main subject, the clerkships locally: a major feature of the Medical University of Gdansk is that it is divided into the Polish Division and the English Division. Nagoya University students are assigned to the latter. During the clerkships, the doctors and patients are of course Polish, but the members of the clerkship groups were all students who had come all the way here from abroad at university entrance, such as Swedes and Indians. Because everything except history-taking from relatively elderly patients with whom English communication was difficult was conducted in English, the hurdle to understanding what is happening in front of you is lowered a step, which is the good point of this university's program. And the students of this English Division were, as one would expect of people who have gone abroad for university, very proactive and truly kind. Japanese people are extremely rare to them and many are anime fans, so they were interested and asked me various questions. In the 11 weeks of clerkships, the department rotated basically every week, and in many departments there was a simple written exam on Friday, and they shared past exams and test-preparation materials, and after the exams we simply talked at a nearby food court or cafe, and I felt truly blessed with good companions.
Here I would like to pick two of the departments I rotated through that I especially remember and describe them briefly.

First was Endocrinology, which I did in the first week. The highlight of this department was a seminar in which the doctor brought actual patients into the classroom and the whole clerkship group of 20 or 30 freely took histories and thought about the diagnosed disease. The experience was very fresh, and patients with acromegaly, Addison's disease, Hashimoto's disease (with subsequent hyperprolactinemia), insulinoma and MEN1 came, and I got a realistic image. What I thought was different from Japan was that there are students who speak up proactively regardless of whether they are right or wrong. They basically do not raise their hands, and there is certainly no case of the teacher naming a student to answer. I truly felt I wanted to follow that proactivity.

Next was Toxicology and emergency states in internal medicine, which I did in the sixth week. The clerkship was held at the Toxicology center in the city center, a little away from the university. In small groups of about five we took histories from several inpatients, and what I saw included, for example, an 18-year-old girl who had overdosed on lamotrigine out of stress from various relationships, lost consciousness and been hospitalised. This girl could speak English, so when I took the history of a middle-aged patient in the same room she even interpreted for me, which was truly helpful. I think this is a sight that can hardly be seen in Japan. Learning the circumstances of each patient's overdose also amounts to prying into that person's life, and I became quite nervous, but every patient was cooperative and it was a very valuable opportunity.

One day during the Easter holidays, as the day of my return approached, an Indian student I had become friends with in the clerkship group said this to me: "You came here by yourself, and you're going back with us in your mind." I suddenly felt keenly that I would soon leave the scene spreading out before me, and that I had certainly lived 11 weeks in this place. During this study abroad I sometimes asked myself what on earth had changed in me, but I realised that, through countless encounters, I was already preserving those memories and learning only within myself. And with these memories and learnings, I felt that color would be added to my life from now on. Expectation sprouted that I would again be able to work hard toward something with a fresh feeling. That feeling of "LIFE IS COMING BACK" at that time, those words still echo in my heart even now.
Finally, I deeply thank everyone, beginning with the professors of the International Collaboration Office, who gave great support for this study abroad. Thank you.
